name: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
title: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
answer: Obligation and service level tracking covers identifying, recording, and monitoring commitments in contracts, such as delivery dates, uptime percentages, response times, renewal windows, payment milestones, and regulatory duties. It sits within contract lifecycle management and algorithmic drafting, where AI reads executed agreements and turns clauses into structured obligations with owners, due dates, and thresholds. The scope includes both affirmative duties and service level agreements, plus exceptions and remedies when a metric is missed. The goal is a live register of what each party must do, not a static archive.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Obligation and service level tracking covers identifying, recording, and monitoring commitments in contracts, such as delivery dates, uptime percentages, response times, renewal windows, payment milestones, and regulatory duties. It sits within contract lifecycle management and algorithmic drafting, where AI reads executed agreements and turns clauses into structured obligations with owners, due dates, and thresholds. The scope includes both affirmative duties and service level agreements, plus exceptions and remedies when a metric is missed. The goal is a live register of what each party must do, not a static archive.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on contract lifecycle management platforms that store source documents and metadata, connected to calendars, ticketing, billing, and monitoring systems. The AI layer uses document parsers, clause classifiers, and extraction models, often fine-tuned on legal text, plus a rules engine for thresholds and recurrence. Data may live in a cloud tenant with role-based access, audit logs, and versioned contract records. Some deployments keep the model inside the customer's environment for confidentiality.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The system ingests signed PDFs or Word files, splits them into clauses, and classifies each clause by obligation type. Extraction models pull parties, dates, amounts, percentages, and service level targets, then a human reviewer confirms or corrects the structured fields. Once confirmed, the tracker compares actual performance data, such as uptime logs or ticket timestamps, against the contractual threshold and raises an alert on breach or near-breach. Recurring obligations are scheduled, and amendments re-trigger extraction so the register stays current.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Every extracted obligation should carry a pointer back to the exact clause and contract version, so an auditor can see why an alert fired. Access controls limit who can edit confirmed obligations, and changes are logged. Risk arises from silent extraction errors, stale source documents, and over-reliance on automated alerts without human review. Data protection terms in the underlying contracts may restrict where performance data can be processed, and the tracker itself may become evidence in a dispute, so retention and deletion rules matter.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Tracking is moving from periodic manual review to continuous monitoring tied to operational systems, with alerts that predict a likely miss before the deadline. Algorithmic drafting will feed negotiated service levels directly into the tracker, reducing re-keying and mismatch. Expect more standardized obligation schemas and clause libraries that make extraction more reliable across vendors. The harder open question is liability and process when an automated tracker misses an obligation, which will push firms toward defined human sign-off and model validation routines.
